title: The Peacock and the Crane
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Peacock taunted a Crane with the dullness of her plumage. "Look at my brilliant colours," said she, "and see how much finer they are than your poor feathers." "I am not denying," replied the Crane, "that yours are far gayer than mine; but when it comes to flying I can soar into the clouds, whereas you are confined to the earth like any dunghill cock."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Peacock taunt the Crane about?
options: Her inability to fly at all

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Peacock tell the Crane to look at?
According to the passage, what does the Peacock call the Crane's feathers?
According to the passage, what does the Crane admit about the Peacock's colours?
options: That they are far gayer than her own
That they fade quickly in sunlight
That they are not really that impressive
That they are the same as her own

questions.prompt: According to the Crane, what can she do that the Peacock cannot?
According to the Crane, to what is the Peacock confined?
options: The earth, like any dunghill cock

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "taunted" mean in "A Peacock taunted a Crane"?
Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Peacocks are more admired than any other bird
A striking appearance is worth less than a genuinely useful ability
Cranes cannot compete with peacocks in any way
Flying is less important than having colourful feathers

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who speaks first in the exchange?
options: Both speak at the same time

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what phrase does the Crane use to begin her reply?
According to the passage, what does the Crane compare the earthbound Peacock to?
As the passage uses it, what does "gayer" mean in "yours are far gayer than mine"?
Based on the passage, why does the Crane bring up her ability to fly?
options: To show that a plain appearance can come with an ability the showier Peacock lacks
To prove that flying matters more to Peacocks than to Cranes
To suggest the Peacock should learn to fly instead of walking
To admit that she wishes she had the Peacock's feathers instead

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Peacock mocks a Crane's plain feathers, but the Crane points out she can fly while the Peacock is grounded
A Crane mocks a Peacock's dull feathers until the Peacock proves her wrong
A Peacock and a Crane agree that appearance matters more than any other quality
A Crane refuses to speak to a Peacock who insults her
